extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and the research integrity community
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards relevant to deciding when published biomedical research should be corrected or retracted, focused on findings of fabrication/falsification, omissions, institutional responsibility, and timeliness of correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains fabrication and falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Swedish National Board for Assessment of Research Misconduct concluded the paper “contains fabrication and falsification in several places.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding that a paper contains fabrication or falsification is grounds for retraction; the page cites the board’s investigation leading directly to The Lancet retracting the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsified figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation found “three falsified figures (4, 5 and 6C).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific identification of falsified figures in an article is treated as a serious form of falsification and supports retraction of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting material information can constitute falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: The board found that the statement that a “4-month follow-up showed no complications” and that omitting information that a stent was inserted constitutes falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate or misleading omission of key clinical facts (e.g., insertion of a stent shortly after the operation) can be judged as falsification, not merely poor reporting, and justify corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions of concern as preliminary corrective step
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lancet issued two Expressions of concern in February, 2023 for the original case description and the 5-year follow-up Article before retracting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may issue expressions of concern while investigations proceed; such notices often precede retraction when investigations confirm misconduct or serious errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent investigation findings justify retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation by the Swedish National Board for Assessment of Research Misconduct into the paper led to the journal retracting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal findings of national or institutional bodies that conclude misconduct (fabrication/falsification) are decisive evidence journals rely on when deciding to retract articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of correction/retraction matters to journal reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics noted concern that the decision to retract took more than 5 years since the Lancet received irrefutable evidence, harming the journal’s reputation for correcting the scientific record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant delay between evidence of falsehood/misconduct and retraction is criticized and seen as damaging to trust in journals; prompt correction is implied as a quality expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior authors and institutions share responsibility to address false papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers argued that other senior authors and their institutions have known for some years that the article is false and that institutions (e.g., UCL re: Martin Birchall) should act to retract or investigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-authors and affiliated institutions are expected to investigate and, where appropriate, request or support retraction; failure to do so is critiqued as institutional negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/oversight requirements (IRB/clinical trial) are relevant to assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters said this is the result of not having an IRB and/or clinical trial and questioned why oversight committees did not find complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of proper ethical oversight or clinical-trial framework for interventions that affect patients is treated as a serious procedural failing that bears on the legitimacy and safety of reported work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of clinical outcome statements must be verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: The articles claimed the patient “had a normal social and working life” and that the graft provided a functional airway and improved quality of life at 4 months—claims later contradicted by evidence of complications and further surgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims about patient outcomes and functional success must be supported by verifiable clinical evidence; demonstrably false claims about outcomes can amount to grounds for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should correct the scientific record when evidence is irrefutable
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction Watch and commentators emphasise that once irrefutable evidence shows an article is false, journals must correct the record (retract) rather than ignore requests from clinicians, scientists, and oversight bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial responsibility includes acting on clear evidence of falsity; reluctance to retract despite clear proof is criticized and seen as failing to maintain the integrity of the literature.
